title: Atlas Ladder
basedOn: Ayn Rand’s philosophy, organized by topic. Short quotations are from her own works and are listed in SOURCES.md.

sections.title: Metaphysics
sections.summary: What exists, and what it is to exist. Volition is the top floor of this section, after the axioms, primacy, causality, and the metaphysically given.

units.title: Existence, Identity, Consciousness
units.summary: The three axioms and the formulas that state them.

lessons.title: Where philosophy starts
lessons.objective: Name Objectivism, the one-foot branches, and the three axiomatic concepts.

lessons.title: Existence exists
lessons.objective: Hold the first axiom: something is, and it does not depend on a wish.

lessons.title: A is A
lessons.objective: To exist is to be something. A contradiction is an error in thinking, not a feature of reality.

lessons.title: Consciousness
lessons.objective: Consciousness perceives what exists. Awareness with no object cancels itself.

lessons.title: One set of axioms
lessons.objective: Hold the three formulas together, and see why causality and primacy come next.

units.title: Primacy of Existence
units.summary: The universe exists independent of consciousness. Consciousness apprehends. It does not decree.

lessons.title: Independent of consciousness
lessons.objective: State that the universe exists whether or not anyone is aware of it.

lessons.title: Consciousness apprehends
lessons.objective: Say what consciousness does: it takes in what exists. It does not create it.

lessons.title: It does not decree
lessons.objective: Reject the idea that wishing, believing, or agreeing can rewrite what exists.

lessons.title: Two opposite claims
lessons.objective: Tell primacy of existence apart from the claim that consciousness comes first and sets the facts.

lessons.title: Hold the unit
lessons.objective: Put the three lines together: independent existence, apprehension, and no decree.

units.title: Causality as a Corollary of Identity
units.summary: The law of causality as the law of identity applied to action. A fuller floor than the preview you just climbed.

lessons.title: Identity applied to action
lessons.objective: State the law of causality as the law of identity applied to action, not as a second rule beside identity.

lessons.title: The entities that act
lessons.objective: Locate the cause in the nature of the entities that act, not in a push with no thing behind it.

lessons.title: No action against its nature
lessons.objective: Hold that a thing cannot act in contradiction to its nature, while still allowing action that fits what it is.

lessons.title: Not a rival law
lessons.objective: Reject substitutes that treat causality as chance, decree, or a second axiom that can break identity.

lessons.title: The fuller floor
lessons.objective: Connect the short formula to the longer clause and treat them as one statement, fuller than the preview.

units.title: The Metaphysically Given
units.summary: Facts that are, as against facts that human choice brings into existence. What is given is not up for a vote.

lessons.title: Facts that are
lessons.objective: Name a metaphysically given fact as something that is, not something a person decided to create.

lessons.title: Brought into existence by choice
lessons.objective: Identify facts that exist because human choice brought them into existence.

lessons.title: Not up for a vote
lessons.objective: See that a metaphysically given fact is not settled by a vote, a poll, or a majority.

lessons.title: A wish is not the given
lessons.objective: Separate wanting a fact to be otherwise from the metaphysically given fact itself.

lessons.title: Hold both sides
lessons.objective: Sort mixed cases by keeping facts that are on one side and facts that choice brings into existence on the other.

units.title: Volition
units.summary: The primary choice to focus or not, and volition as axiomatic. This ladder places it after the metaphysically given.

lessons.title: The primary choice
lessons.objective: Name the primary act of volition: the choice to focus the mind or not to focus it.

lessons.title: Focus before content
lessons.objective: Separate the effort of focus from later choices about what to think, say, or do.

lessons.title: Volition is axiomatic
lessons.objective: Explain why volition is axiomatic: an attempt to deny the choice already uses it.

lessons.title: After the metaphysically given
lessons.objective: Place volition after the metaphysically given: what is given is not chosen, and choice is what can add man-made facts.

lessons.title: Given, then the axiom
lessons.objective: Hold the unit in one order: the metaphysically given, the primary choice to focus or not, and volition as axiomatic.

units.title: Entities and Their Actions
units.summary: To exist is to be an entity of a specific nature. Action follows from what the entity is.

lessons.title: To be something
lessons.objective: Recognize that to exist is to be something, set against the nothing of nonexistence.

lessons.title: An entity
lessons.objective: Identify what exists as an entity, not as a loose feature floating free of any thing.

lessons.title: A specific nature
lessons.objective: State that an entity has a specific nature, not an open character that can be anything.

lessons.title: Specific attributes
lessons.objective: Connect an entity’s nature to the specific attributes that make that nature up.

lessons.title: Action follows
lessons.objective: Explain that what an entity does follows from what that entity is, not from a demand that ignores its nature.

units.title: Existence as the Total
units.summary: There is nothing outside existence. The universe is everything that exists.

lessons.title: Nothing outside
lessons.objective: State that there is nothing outside existence: whatever is, is inside existence.

lessons.title: Everything that exists
lessons.objective: Define the universe as everything that exists, not as one object among other objects.

lessons.title: Nonexistence is not a place
lessons.objective: Reject treating nonexistence as a region, a background, or a somewhere beyond what exists.

lessons.title: No larger container
lessons.objective: See that existence is not inside a bigger frame, void, or second total.

lessons.title: Hold the two lines
lessons.objective: Hold both lines together: nothing is outside existence, and the universe is everything that exists.

sections.title: Epistemology
sections.summary: How you know. This section starts with the senses. Volition is on the metaphysics ladder.

units.title: The Validity of the Senses
units.summary: The senses as your only direct contact, percepts as the given, and the stolen-concept trap in attacking them.

lessons.title: The only direct contact
lessons.objective: The senses provide the material. Reason integrates it. Emotions do not replace either.

lessons.title: Percepts are the given
lessons.objective: You are aware of entities, not of free-floating sensations stored one by one.

lessons.title: The senses do not invent
lessons.objective: The organs have no volition to distort. The mind still has to identify what they give.

lessons.title: The stolen concept
lessons.objective: An attack on the senses that uses sensory evidence has stolen its own base.

lessons.title: From percept to reason
lessons.objective: Put the unit in one order: material, percept, identification, truth.

units.title: Concept-Formation and Measurement-Omission
units.summary: Differentiation, integration, and concepts as a mathematical process of measurement-omission.

lessons.title: Set the group apart
lessons.objective: Isolate units by what they share with each other and how they differ from a wider background.

lessons.title: Unite the units
lessons.objective: Integrate the isolated units into one new mental entity, the concept.

lessons.title: Same characteristic, different measure
lessons.objective: Treat similarity as the same characteristic possessed in different measure, so the process is mathematical.

lessons.title: Omit the particular measurements
lessons.objective: Form the concept by retaining the characteristic and omitting the particular measurements.

lessons.title: One mathematical process
lessons.objective: Run differentiation, integration, and measurement-omission as one ordered process that yields a concept.

units.title: Definitions and the Hierarchy
units.summary: Definition as the last step of concept-formation, and concepts as a hierarchy rather than a pile.

lessons.title: The last step
lessons.objective: Place a definition after concept-formation: the units are integrated first, and the definition then states what kind they are.

lessons.title: Genus and differentia
lessons.objective: Build a definition from a genus, the wider group, and a differentia, the characteristic that sets these units apart inside that group.

lessons.title: The fundamental characteristic
lessons.objective: Select the fundamental distinguishing characteristic, the one that explains the others, rather than a surface mark.

lessons.title: A hierarchy, not a pile
lessons.objective: Treat concepts as a hierarchy in which later concepts rest on earlier ones, not as a flat pile of labels.

lessons.title: Context and the same units
lessons.objective: See that a definition states the fundamentals in the order of one's knowledge, and can be restated when that knowledge deepens without dropping the units.

units.title: Objectivity
units.summary: Volitional adherence to reality by the method of logic. Knowledge as contextual and hierarchical.

lessons.title: Adherence to reality
lessons.objective: State objectivity as a chosen adherence to the facts, not as neutrality and not as a mind that writes reality.

lessons.title: The method of logic
lessons.objective: Identify logic as the method of objectivity: non-contradictory identification of the facts.

lessons.title: A choice to adhere
lessons.objective: Separate what is given in awareness from the choice to adhere to it by logic.

lessons.title: Knowledge in context
lessons.objective: Treat a conclusion as holding in the context of the evidence that supports it, and treat context-dropping as a failure of objectivity.

lessons.title: Knowledge in an order
lessons.objective: Treat knowledge as hierarchical: later conclusions rest on earlier ones and cannot replace the base they depend on.

units.title: Reason, Mysticism, and Skepticism
units.summary: Reason as the only means of knowledge, and mysticism and skepticism as denials of it.

lessons.title: The only means of knowledge
lessons.objective: Reason is the only means of knowledge and the only standard of truth.

lessons.title: Mysticism
lessons.objective: Mysticism claims a way of knowing that bypasses reason, such as faith, revelation, or feeling used as proof.

lessons.title: Skepticism
lessons.objective: Skepticism denies that knowledge is possible, and so denies that reason succeeds.

lessons.title: What rejecting reason licenses
lessons.objective: Rejecting reason means acting with no regard for the facts, or against them.

lessons.title: Three answers about knowledge
lessons.objective: Sort reason, mysticism, and skepticism by what each says about whether and how you can know.

units.title: Certainty and the Arbitrary
units.summary: The arbitrary as neither true nor false, and certainty as contextual.

lessons.title: A claim with nothing behind it
lessons.objective: Recognize an arbitrary assertion as a claim offered with no evidence and no tie to the facts you know.

lessons.title: Neither true nor false
lessons.objective: Treat the arbitrary as cognitively empty: it is neither true nor false, so it is set aside instead of weighed as a candidate.

lessons.title: Who must offer evidence
lessons.objective: Place the burden of proof on the person who asserts, and refuse the demand to disprove a claim that was never supported.

lessons.title: Certainty inside a context
lessons.objective: Explain certainty as knowing that, inside a given context of evidence, nothing warrants doubt, without claiming to know every fact outside that context.

lessons.title: Possibility is not a shrug
lessons.objective: Separate a genuine possibility, which some evidence supports, from an arbitrary maybe that cannot undercut contextual certainty.

units.title: Logic
units.summary: Logic as the art of non-contradictory identification.

lessons.title: The art itself
lessons.objective: State logic as the art of identifying what is, and of keeping those identifications free of contradiction.

lessons.title: Identify what is
lessons.objective: Treat logic as naming facts that are already there, not as inventing them or swapping them for a wish.

lessons.title: Not both at once
lessons.objective: Apply non-contradiction: the same thing cannot be two incompatible things at the same time and in the same respect.

lessons.title: The error is in the thinking
lessons.objective: Treat a contradiction as a confession that your thinking went wrong, not as a discovery that reality contradicts itself.

lessons.title: Do not keep the clash
lessons.objective: Distinguish finding a contradiction, which exposes an error, from maintaining it, which gives up the mind's hold on the facts.

units.title: Context and Hierarchy
units.summary: Knowledge is contextual and hierarchical. A concept used with no context is floating.

lessons.title: Knowledge has a context
lessons.objective: Explain a context of knowledge as the body of facts and earlier ideas a claim depends on, not as a mood or a private story.

lessons.title: Knowledge has an order
lessons.objective: Describe hierarchy as an order in which later knowledge rests on earlier knowledge and cannot be used as if it came first.

lessons.title: A concept with no context
lessons.objective: Identify a floating concept as one used with no context, cut off from the facts and the order that give it a meaning.

lessons.title: Put the concept back
lessons.objective: Restore a concept by naming the facts it refers to and the earlier knowledge it rests on, instead of adding emphasis.

lessons.title: One check, two questions
lessons.objective: Apply context and hierarchy together: ask what knowledge the concept depends on, and whether that knowledge is earlier in the order.

sections.title: Human Nature
sections.summary: What kind of organism a human being is, once metaphysics and epistemology are in place.

units.title: Man as a Rational Animal
units.summary: Living organisms as goal-directed, and reason as the human means of survival.

lessons.title: Life aims at itself
lessons.objective: See a living organism as an entity whose actions are directed at keeping itself alive.

lessons.title: No built-in survival code
lessons.objective: Contrast automatic living action in plants and animals with the fact that a human being has no innate program for how to survive.

lessons.title: Reason is the means
lessons.objective: Identify reason as the human means of survival: the faculty that identifies and integrates what the senses provide.

lessons.title: Reason has to be used
lessons.objective: Hold that reason does not run by itself: surviving by it takes the choice to think and to act on what you know.

lessons.title: One picture of the rational animal
lessons.objective: Put the unit in one order: a goal-directed organism, no innate survival code, and reason as the means you must use.

units.title: Mind and Body
units.summary: No war between a ghostly mind and a mechanical body. Reason is an attribute of the individual.

lessons.title: The war that is not there
lessons.objective: Name the false picture: a ghostly mind at war with a mechanical body.

lessons.title: One individual
lessons.objective: Hold mind and body as aspects of one individual, not two rivals sharing a life.

lessons.title: Reason belongs to the person
lessons.objective: Place reason as an attribute of the individual, not of a spirit world or a crowd.

lessons.title: No ghostly mind
lessons.objective: Deny that the mind is a disembodied ghost occupying a body.

lessons.title: No mechanical body
lessons.objective: Deny that the body is a mindless machine the mind must conquer.

units.title: Emotions as Products of Ideas
units.summary: Emotions as consequences of value-judgments, not as tools that discover facts.

lessons.title: Products of ideas
lessons.objective: See an emotion as a consequence of a value-judgment you already hold, not as a first fact about the world.

lessons.title: An estimate, not the facts
lessons.objective: Distinguish what a feeling reports — your estimate of the facts — from what it does not report: the facts themselves.

lessons.title: Not a tool that discovers facts
lessons.objective: Reject the claim that emotions are tools of cognition — means that discover facts.

lessons.title: The judgment comes first
lessons.objective: Trace the order: idea and value-judgment, then emotion. The feeling does not come first and then invent the judgment.

lessons.title: When feeling and fact clash
lessons.objective: When a feeling and a fact conflict, re-check the value-judgment instead of treating the feeling as evidence.

units.title: Free Will and Character
units.summary: Character as the self you build by the choices you automate. A later floor, not a substitute for volition.

lessons.title: The self you build
lessons.objective: Name character as the self you build, not a finished self you are handed.

lessons.title: Choices you automate
lessons.objective: Show that character is formed when choices are repeated until they run as a standing policy.

lessons.title: A later floor
lessons.objective: Place character after volition: a later floor, not the base of the ladder.

lessons.title: Not a substitute
lessons.objective: Show that an automated character does not stand in for the choice you still have.

lessons.title: Will, then character
lessons.objective: Hold the unit in one order: free will first, then the self those choices make automatic.

units.title: Needs of a Living Being
units.summary: A living organism's needs follow from the kind of organism it is. Man's needs include the use of reason.

lessons.title: What a need is
lessons.objective: Identify a need as something required by the kind of living organism, not a whim or a luxury.

lessons.title: The kind sets the needs
lessons.objective: Show that different kinds of organism have different needs, because each need follows from the kind of organism it is.

lessons.title: Man's kind, man's needs
lessons.objective: Apply the rule to man: his needs are the needs of the kind of organism he is, not a list taken from another kind.

lessons.title: The need to use reason
lessons.objective: Place the use of reason among man’s needs, as a requirement of the kind of organism he is, not as an optional extra.

lessons.title: Needs in one picture
lessons.objective: Hold the unit in one order: a living organism’s needs follow from the kind of organism it is, and man’s needs include the use of reason.

units.title: Man Among Men
units.summary: Other people can be a value in a voluntary relationship. Society is not an organism that owns the individual.

lessons.title: Other people can be a value
lessons.objective: See that another person can be a value to you, not a threat merely by existing.

lessons.title: A voluntary relationship
lessons.objective: Hold that the value of other people is a relationship both people choose, not a tie that is forced.

lessons.title: Not an organism
lessons.objective: Reject the picture of society as a living organism with a life of its own above the people in it.

lessons.title: It does not own you
lessons.objective: Deny that society owns the individual or may treat a person as its property.

lessons.title: Value, not ownership
lessons.objective: Hold both claims at once: other people can be a value in a voluntary relationship, and society is not an organism that owns the individual.

sections.title: Ethics
sections.summary: The code that guides choices, once you know what you are and how you know.

units.title: Why Man Needs Morality
units.summary: Why a code of values is a requirement of human life, not a decoration.

lessons.title: A code of values
lessons.objective: Name morality as a code of values that guides choices and actions, not a mood or a slogan.

lessons.title: Why human life requires it
lessons.objective: Explain why a being who must choose needs a code of values, while a life of automatic action does not.

lessons.title: Not a decoration
lessons.objective: Reject the idea that morality is an optional ornament, a luxury, or something added only after life is secure.

lessons.title: Without a code
lessons.objective: See that without a code, choices have no standard, so action drifts by whim and is not a policy for living.

lessons.title: The reason, held together
lessons.objective: State the full claim: man needs morality because a code of values is required to choose the actions human life depends on, and that need is not decorative.

units.title: Life as the Standard
units.summary: Life as the root of value, and one’s own life as the standard of moral value.

lessons.title: Why Value Needs Life
lessons.objective: Recognize that the idea of value depends on a living being that can gain or lose its existence.

lessons.title: The Alternative That Makes Good and Evil
lessons.objective: Explain that good and evil arise only where the alternative is life or death.

lessons.title: Not a Whim or a Command
lessons.objective: Reject whim, crowd opinion, and a supernatural command as the root of value.

lessons.title: One's Own Life as the Standard
lessons.objective: Identify one's own life as the standard used to judge moral good and evil for oneself.

lessons.title: For or Against That Life
lessons.objective: Judge an action as morally good when it sustains one's own life and as morally evil when it works against that life.

units.title: The Three Cardinal Values
units.summary: Reason, purpose, and self-esteem.

lessons.title: Name the three
lessons.objective: Name reason, purpose, and self-esteem as the three cardinal values, and say what cardinal means.

lessons.title: Reason as a value
lessons.objective: Explain reason as the cardinal value that makes knowledge and chosen action possible.

lessons.title: Purpose
lessons.objective: Explain purpose as a chosen central goal that ranks a person's other values.

lessons.title: Self-esteem
lessons.objective: Explain self-esteem as the earned conviction that one is competent to think and worthy of living.

lessons.title: One set
lessons.objective: Hold reason, purpose, and self-esteem as one set, and see how each depends on the other two.

units.title: The Seven Virtues
units.summary: Rationality, independence, integrity, honesty, justice, productiveness, and pride.

lessons.title: Name the seven
lessons.objective: Name the seven virtues in the unit’s order and keep them as one code.

lessons.title: Rationality first
lessons.objective: Treat rationality as the virtue of using reason to know the facts and to choose.

lessons.title: Independence and integrity
lessons.objective: Separate thinking for yourself from acting on the judgment you have reached.

lessons.title: Honesty and justice
lessons.objective: Contrast refusing to fake reality with judging people by the facts of what they do.

lessons.title: Productiveness and pride
lessons.objective: Connect making values with the moral ambition to be worthy of your own life.

units.title: Happiness
units.summary: Happiness as the emotional state that follows from achieved values, not as a whim.

lessons.title: An Emotional State
lessons.objective: Identify happiness as an emotional state, not a possession, a rule, or a mood you invent.

lessons.title: What It Follows From
lessons.objective: Connect the emotional state of happiness to values that have been achieved.

lessons.title: Achievement Comes First
lessons.objective: Keep the order straight: the value is achieved, and the emotional state follows.

lessons.title: Not a Whim
lessons.objective: Separate happiness from a whim, a feeling with no tie to achieved values.

lessons.title: The Whole Definition
lessons.objective: State the full idea in one piece: the emotional state that follows achieved values, and not a whim.

units.title: Egoism and Altruism
units.summary: The individual as the proper beneficiary of his own action, against the demand that he live for others.

lessons.title: Who the action is for
lessons.objective: Name the individual himself as the proper beneficiary of his own action.

lessons.title: The demand to live for others
lessons.objective: Identify the moral demand this unit rejects: that a person live for others.

lessons.title: What altruism asks
lessons.objective: Describe altruism, in this contrast, as the code that makes others the beneficiary of one’s action.

lessons.title: Action and its proper gain
lessons.objective: Connect a concrete action to the person who properly gains from it, and reject handing that gain away as a duty.

lessons.title: Hold the contrast
lessons.objective: Keep egoism and the rejected demand distinct when the wording changes.

units.title: The Trader Principle
units.summary: Give value for value. Do not seek the unearned.

lessons.title: Give value for value
lessons.objective: State the trader principle as an exchange in which each person gives a value and receives a value.

lessons.title: Both sides gain
lessons.objective: Explain that a trade is an exchange in which each person gains a value, so neither is asked to lose for the other.

lessons.title: Do not seek the unearned
lessons.objective: Identify the unearned as a value one seeks without giving a value in return, and reject that aim.

lessons.title: Trade is not taking
lessons.objective: Tell a trade apart from taking, from a one-sided demand, and from payment that does not match a value given.

lessons.title: Both clauses together
lessons.objective: Hold the full rule: give value for value, and do not seek the unearned, including when a case looks mixed.

units.title: Sacrifice
units.summary: Sacrifice as giving up a higher value for a lesser one, and why that is not a virtue on this ladder.

lessons.title: What sacrifice names
lessons.objective: Define sacrifice, on this ladder, as giving up a higher value for a lesser one.

lessons.title: Not every cost
lessons.objective: Separate a cost paid to gain a higher value from sacrifice as this unit defines it.

lessons.title: Not a virtue
lessons.objective: Explain why giving up a higher value for a lesser one is not a virtue on this ladder.

lessons.title: Rank decides
lessons.objective: Use the rank of two values to decide whether a trade is a sacrifice.

lessons.title: The claim together
lessons.objective: State the whole unit: sacrifice is giving up a higher value for a lesser one, and that is not a virtue.

sections.title: Politics
sections.summary: The social principles that follow when each person is an end in himself.

units.title: Individual Rights
units.summary: Rights as principles that sanction freedom of action in a social context.

lessons.title: What a right is
lessons.objective: Identify a right as a principle that sanctions a person's freedom of action.

lessons.title: A social context
lessons.objective: Place rights among people, not in a person's dealings with nature or with himself alone.

lessons.title: Freedom of action
lessons.objective: Distinguish the freedom a right sanctions from a claim on other people's effort or goods.

lessons.title: Not a permission
lessons.objective: Contrast a right with a permission or privilege that others can grant or withdraw.

lessons.title: Rights as principles
lessons.objective: Treat rights as moral principles that set a standard, not as wishes, customs, or majority votes.

units.title: The Initiation of Force
units.summary: Why starting the use of physical force is the basic political evil.

lessons.title: What physical force is
lessons.objective: Name physical force as compulsion against a person’s body or property, not as a strong opinion.

lessons.title: Who starts it
lessons.objective: Separate the person who starts force from the person who uses force only to stop it.

lessons.title: Why it is basic
lessons.objective: Explain why starting force is the basic political evil: it replaces the victim’s judgment with compulsion.

lessons.title: Fraud and threats
lessons.objective: Treat fraud and a credible threat of force as ways of starting force, not as clever exceptions.

lessons.title: What is not a start of force
lessons.objective: Keep refusal, competition, error, and unwelcome speech outside the idea of starting force.

units.title: Government’s Proper Role
units.summary: Government as an agent that protects rights, limited to retaliatory force.

lessons.title: An agent, not a master
lessons.objective: Identify government as an agent that acts for people, not as an owner of their lives.

lessons.title: The job: protect rights
lessons.objective: State the purpose of government as the protection of individual rights, and reject substitute purposes.

lessons.title: Only retaliatory force
lessons.objective: Limit the force government may use to retaliation against those who have started force.

lessons.title: Police, courts, defense
lessons.objective: Place police, law courts, and armed defense inside the job of protecting rights by retaliatory force.

lessons.title: Where the role stops
lessons.objective: Apply the whole unit: an agent that protects rights and stops where retaliatory force stops.

units.title: Capitalism and Its Moral Basis
units.summary: Laissez-faire capitalism as the system that follows from rights, not as a brute economic preference.

lessons.title: Name the system
lessons.objective: Identify laissez-faire capitalism as the political system this unit defends.

lessons.title: It follows from rights
lessons.objective: Explain that the case for laissez-faire capitalism starts from individual rights.

lessons.title: Not a brute preference
lessons.objective: Reject the idea that capitalism is only a taste for markets or a growth trick.

lessons.title: What laissez-faire rules out
lessons.objective: State what laissez-faire rules out: running the economy and handing out special favors.

lessons.title: One chain
lessons.objective: Hold one order: each person is an end, rights follow, and laissez-faire capitalism is the system that respects those rights.

units.title: Property Rights
units.summary: The right to keep and use the product of your effort, and why freedom of action requires it.

lessons.title: What property is
lessons.objective: Name property as the right to keep and use the product of your effort.

lessons.title: The product of your effort
lessons.objective: Identify what the right covers as the product of your own effort, and reject treating another person's product as yours.

lessons.title: The right to use it
lessons.objective: Treat use as part of the right, and reject a title that forbids the owner to act on what he keeps.

lessons.title: Why freedom of action requires it
lessons.objective: Explain that freedom of action requires property, because action needs control of its means and of its result.

lessons.title: The whole claim
lessons.objective: Apply the full unit: the right to keep and use the product of your effort, because freedom of action requires that control.

units.title: Statism
units.summary: The political view that a person's life belongs to the state.

lessons.title: Name the view
lessons.objective: Identify statism as the political view that a person's life belongs to the state.

lessons.title: Who the owner is
lessons.objective: Name the state, not the person, as the owner statism assigns to a life.

lessons.title: What the life covers
lessons.objective: Treat the life that statism assigns to the state as including the person's work, time, and choices.

lessons.title: The person as a means
lessons.objective: Explain that statism treats the person as a means to the state's ends because the life belongs to the state.

lessons.title: Spot the wording
lessons.objective: Recognize the same statism claim when it is worded as a duty to the state, a national purpose, or the public's ownership of the person.

sections.title: Aesthetics
sections.summary: Art as a need of a conceptual consciousness, and the standards for judging it.

units.title: Art as Selective Re-creation
units.summary: Art as a selective re-creation of reality according to metaphysical value-judgments.

lessons.title: What Art Is
lessons.objective: State the definition of art as a selective re-creation of reality according to metaphysical value-judgments.

lessons.title: What Selective Means
lessons.objective: Explain that the artist includes, omits, and stresses aspects of reality rather than recording everything.

lessons.title: Re-creation, Not a Dump or a Fantasy
lessons.objective: Distinguish a re-creation of reality from an unselective record and from a presentation cut off from reality.

lessons.title: Metaphysical Value-Judgments
lessons.objective: Identify metaphysical value-judgments as the artist’s fundamental appraisal of man and existence, and as the standard of selection.

lessons.title: One Claim, Three Parts
lessons.objective: Apply the full definition, keeping selection, re-creation of reality, and metaphysical value-judgments together.

units.title: Sense of Life
units.summary: A sense of life as a pre-conceptual, emotional appraisal of man and of existence.

lessons.title: What the phrase names
lessons.objective: Name a sense of life as a pre-conceptual, emotional appraisal, and reject the usual substitutes.

lessons.title: An appraisal of man
lessons.objective: Identify man as one object of the appraisal: what kind of being one takes a human being to be.

lessons.title: An appraisal of existence
lessons.objective: Identify existence as the other object: an emotional estimate of the world a human being faces.

lessons.title: Before a stated philosophy
lessons.objective: Hold that the appraisal is in place before it is translated into explicit ideas, without treating the feeling as a proof.

lessons.title: The emotional whole
lessons.objective: Assemble the full definition: an emotional appraisal that is pre-conceptual and aimed at both man and existence.

units.title: Romanticism
units.summary: Romanticism as the school committed to volition, and its place in Rand’s esthetics.

lessons.title: Where a school sits
lessons.objective: Locate Romanticism as a school inside esthetics, named by its view of man, not by a feeling.

lessons.title: The premise of volition
lessons.objective: State the premise that defines Romanticism: man can choose.

lessons.title: Against the denial of choice
lessons.objective: Tell Romanticism from the school that presents man as determined.

lessons.title: Not a mood
lessons.objective: Separate Romanticism from the popular mix-up with emotion, mysticism, or escape from facts.

lessons.title: What the premise makes visible
lessons.objective: Connect the volitional premise to purposeful action in art, and to why the school belongs in her esthetics.

units.title: Esthetic Judgment
units.summary: How to judge a work by what it does as art, which is not the same as agreeing with its philosophy.

lessons.title: Two different questions
lessons.objective: Separate an esthetic judgment of a work from a philosophical agreement with its ideas.

lessons.title: What the work does as art
lessons.objective: Judge by the selective re-creation the work actually presents, not by a slogan placed beside it.

lessons.title: Skill is not a vote
lessons.objective: See that artistic skill and agreement with a philosophy can come apart in either direction.

lessons.title: Theme through the means
lessons.objective: Ask whether the theme is carried by the work’s own means, rather than by a lecture standing in for the art.

lessons.title: One standard, applied
lessons.objective: Apply the same esthetic standard to works you welcome and works you oppose.

units.title: Why a Conceptual Mind Needs Art
units.summary: Art as a need of a conceptual consciousness, not as a luxury added after thought is finished.

lessons.title: The mind that has the need
lessons.objective: Identify the consciousness that needs art as one that lives by concepts, not by the immediate moment alone.

lessons.title: Not a spare pleasure
lessons.objective: Reject the claim that art is a luxury a person can skip once practical needs are met.

lessons.title: Not attached later
lessons.objective: Reject the picture that thought is finished first and art is attached afterward as decoration.

lessons.title: Why the need arises
lessons.objective: Explain that a conceptual mind needs its wide abstractions in a form it can experience, which is why art is a need.

lessons.title: The claim in one line
lessons.objective: Hold the full claim: art is a need of a conceptual consciousness, not a luxury added after thought is finished.

units.title: Theme
units.summary: A work's abstract meaning, carried by the concretes the artist chose.

lessons.title: What a theme is
lessons.objective: Name a theme as the work's abstract meaning, and reject substitutes that are not a meaning at all.

lessons.title: Not a plot summary
lessons.objective: Tell a theme apart from a retelling of the events, characters, or surface details.

lessons.title: The concretes chosen
lessons.objective: Identify the concretes as the particulars the artist chose, which are what carry the theme.

lessons.title: Carried, not pasted on
lessons.objective: Hold that the theme is carried by the concretes, not supplied by a slogan attached beside them.

lessons.title: One claim
lessons.objective: Apply the full claim: a theme is the work's abstract meaning, and that meaning is carried by the concretes the artist chose.

sections.title: Integration
sections.summary: The philosophy as one whole, and what it asks of a life.

units.title: The Philosophy as a Whole
units.summary: Why an idea pulled out of the middle cannot be validated or used.

lessons.title: One view, not a pile
lessons.objective: Tell an integrated philosophy from a pile of separate claims.

lessons.title: The chain has an order
lessons.objective: See that later ideas rest on earlier ones, so the order is part of the philosophy.

lessons.title: Pulled out of the middle
lessons.objective: Spot an idea that has been cut away from the premises that support it.

lessons.title: Nothing left to check
lessons.objective: Explain why a middle idea, taken alone, cannot be validated.

lessons.title: Nothing left to apply
lessons.objective: Explain why that same detached idea cannot guide a concrete choice.

units.title: Applying It
units.summary: Holding the principles in concrete choices, without turning the philosophy into a script.

lessons.title: Not a script
lessons.objective: Tell a principle from a script: a principle names the kind of choice that is right, and a script pretends the moves are already listed.

lessons.title: This choice
lessons.objective: Apply a principle to the facts of this situation instead of letting a slogan stand in for those facts.

lessons.title: When the facts change
lessons.objective: See that one principle can call for different concrete actions when the facts of the case change.

lessons.title: You still judge
lessons.objective: Use the philosophy as a standard for your thinking, not as a substitute that decides the case in your place.

lessons.title: A life, not a ritual
lessons.objective: Hold the principles across ordinary choices without turning practice into ceremony, costume, or a checklist of gestures.

units.title: Package Deals
units.summary: Two claims glued together so that accepting one seems to force the other.

lessons.title: Two claims, one package
lessons.objective: Recognize a package deal as two claims treated as if they were a single claim.

lessons.title: Find the glue
lessons.objective: Find the word or slogan that hides the join between the two claims.

lessons.title: Name each claim
lessons.objective: Name each claim separately once the package is opened.

lessons.title: One yes is not two
lessons.objective: Judge each claim on its own so that a yes to one is not a yes to the other.

lessons.title: Ask two questions
lessons.objective: Replace the package with two questions you can answer one at a time.

units.title: Check Your Premises
units.summary: When a conclusion clashes with a fact, inspect the premise that produced the conclusion.

lessons.title: Name the clash
lessons.objective: Recognize a clash as a conclusion that does not fit a known fact.

lessons.title: The fact holds
lessons.objective: Keep the fact, and treat the clashing conclusion as the side that has to give.

lessons.title: Trace it back
lessons.objective: Trace the clashing conclusion to the premise that produced it.

lessons.title: Inspect the premise
lessons.objective: Check the producing premise against the fact, instead of shielding it, discarding every idea, or rewriting the fact.

lessons.title: A conclusion that fits
lessons.objective: Replace the faulty premise so the new conclusion agrees with the fact.
